title: Checks first
bridge: Checks first is like test-driven development: write the test, see it red, then make it green. Except: the harness, not the model, runs the red step, and then it locks the test files with a hash. Nova may add tests but never change the ones it is judged by.
intro: This lesson is about proof. Nova reads a checking guide to pick checks and records what it ran and why. It writes each QA check as a failing test before any code. A separate QA agent co-signs the QA plan first, and a hash lock stops Nova from weakening its own checks.

picture.caption: The checks are agreed, written red, and locked before the first line of code.

after approval: where to start checking, when to look deeper
writes one test per QA check at the level the plan names
runs them on unchanged code; each must fail on an assertion
stores a sha256 of each test file
denies Edit or Write on a locked file; the Stop hook re-hashes
writes .nova/checks.json: what ran, why, what was skipped

p: Imagine two tickets. One fixes a typo in a button label. The other renames a serializer field that the SDK reads. A good engineer checks the first in a minute and the second for an hour.
Nova should do the same. A fixed rulebook cannot say which is which. So we write a guide with reasons. It says where to start for each kind of change, when to look deeper, and what proof fits.
This lesson has four pieces. The guide and a record of chosen checks. Then the QA agent that co-signs the plan, and the lock that turns agreed checks into a wall.

The guide is a reference page inside the verify skill, in G8's rhino-core plugin. One short block per kind of change, from docs and FE component to DB migration and dependency bump. Each block says start, look deeper when, and proof.

It uses only commands that exist today. Tools that G7 still has to ship, such as npm run verify and oasdiff, are named as not here yet. The guide says what to do until they land. People read the same page as Nova.
sections.because: Guidance with reasons works better than a fixed rulebook, and one page serves people and agents alike.

code.text:
# Checking guide: where to start, when to look deeper
A starting point, not a rulebook or a timetable. Start from what fits the change, go deeper whenever you see
a reason, and take the time that needs. In the PR, say what you checked, why, and what you chose not to check.
## FE component
- Start: `npm run lint`, `npm run check-types`, the related vitest files, the component's stories in each screen state.
- Look deeper when many pages use it or the layout changes: open those pages at 760 and 1440 (e2e/helpers/responsive.ts).
- Proof: assertions on visible text and ARIA roles; a short video per QA check.
## FE page flow
- Start: the above, plus the Playwright spec for that flow (frontend/e2e/pr/*.spec.ts) on FCP Lab with seed data.
- Look deeper when it touches permissions, data loading or forms: run the neighbouring specs, try the edge cases by hand.
- Proof: the specs ran, a video per check, the Playwright trace.
## BE logic
- Start: pre-commit on the changed files, then `./scripts/local_run_backend_unit_tests.sh cloud rhinoCloud.rhinoCore.tests.<module>`.
- Look deeper when the code is shared, checks permissions, or queries in a loop: run the wider suite and count queries.
- Proof: a new test that failed before the fix and passes after.
## When a check fails
Never weaken it. If main fails the same way, link main's run and say so. A flaky test gets flagged with evidence.
## Not in fcp yet (coming from G7)
`npm run verify`, `poe verify`, testmon, oasdiff, Squawk, kubeconform, zizmor. Until they land, run the parts by hand
and list what you could not run under "What was not checked".

notes.text: The opening sets the tone: a starting point, never a timetable. Depth is Nova's call, with reasons in the PR.
For a component: lint, types, related vitest files and the stories in each screen state.
The sign to look deeper: many pages use it, or the layout changes. Then open pages at 760 and 1440.
A page flow adds the Playwright spec for that flow, run on FCP Lab with seed data.
BE logic starts with pre-commit and the one module's tests through the existing script.
Proof for BE: a new test that failed before the fix and passes after. That is the red-then-green rule.
Never weaken a failing check. If main fails the same way, link main's run as proof it is not yours.
Honest about what is missing. The PR lists what could not be run under its own heading.

sections.h: Check selection: the record behind the PR table
p: Nova writes every check it ran and every check it skipped into .nova/checks.json. Each run has a command, a result and one line of why. It also has a proof key in S3, and the QA check it proves, if any. Each skip has a reason, such as "no visible change, so no browser run".

The PR's checks table (lesson g4-6) is built from this file. The reviewer sees Nova's reasons and can disagree with them. G3's Stop hook reads it too: every QA check in the plan needs a result and proof before Nova may say done.
sections.because: A reviewer can only disagree with a choice they can see, so every run and every skip is recorded with its reason.

notes.text: One check run. The name is what the PR table shows; the command is what Nova typed.
Four results. fails_on_main_too means the failure is not Nova's; main's run is linked as proof.
nullish: the proof may be missing or null, for a lint run that leaves no artifact.
The link back to the plan: QA-2 here means this run is the proof for check QA-2.
The whole record. kind comes from readiness, so the guide block Nova used is clear.
Which compose services Nova started. Empty for a copy change: no app boot for a typo.
Skips are pairs: the check and the reason. Both show in the PR under what was not checked.

sections.h: suggestStart: a starting point, never a gate
p: suggestStart turns the changed paths into a first list of checks and services. Frontend source gets lint, types and the related vitest files. A change under frontend/src/app/ is a page, so the Playwright spec and the app's services join the list. Cloud or client code gets pre-commit and the module's tests.

It only suggests. Nova reads the guide and decides, and nothing stops Nova from adding a check. fcp's compose files have no profiles today, so starting part of the stack goes through FCP Lab. If the Lab cannot, a person adds compose profiles in a small fcp PR.
sections.because: We want Nova to start the right checks without booting the whole app for a copy change. The decision still stays with Nova.

notes.text: Input: the changed paths. Output: suggested checks and services. No side effects.
Frontend source files. Tests and config under frontend/ are not source, so they are left out here.
The three cheap FE checks. --changed origin/main runs the vitest files related to the diff.
A file under frontend/src/app/ is a page or route, so a browser flow is likely affected.
Service names come from cloud/rhinoCloud/docker-compose.yml, so the Lab can start only those.
BE: pre-commit on the changed files, then the one module through fcp's own script.
Returned, not enforced. The caller shows it to Nova as a suggestion.

sections.h: The QA agent co-signs the QA plan
p: Before the plan is posted, a separate QA agent reads only the ticket and the QA plan. It either signs or asks for specific changes. There are six problems: a missing edge case, an unobservable check and a missing screen state. Then class names, the wrong proof, or a check not about the ticket.

It is its own query() session on Sonnet 5.5 at medium, with no tools. It never sees the rest of the plan or Nova's notes, so it cannot be talked into agreeing. Nova revises once; if they still disagree, both views go into the plan message and the requester decides.
The signature (model, time, changes made) is stored in plan.json, and the plan message shows "co-signed by the QA agent".
sections.because: Builder and tester should agree on done before the work starts. And a tester who never saw Nova's reasoning is harder to fool.

notes.text: The harness is bundled, so it imports the SDK from /core (lesson g3-9).
The six problems a QA plan can have. The enum keeps the answer comparable across runs.
sign: true means the plan is good as written. false comes with a list of changes.
check names the QA check to change, or "new" when a check is missing.
The question the QA agent answers: would these checks fail on a broken build?
No tools and no settings: the QA agent reads the two texts and answers. It is not a Nova subagent.
The prompt file seeds it with 4 weak QA plans: no edge case, class names, "the page loads", no error state.
Cosign.parse makes the answer typed. A bad answer throws instead of passing silently.

sections.h: Checks become failing tests, then the lock
p: After approval, Nova writes one test per QA check at the level the plan names. That is vitest in frontend/test/unit/, a Playwright spec in frontend/e2e/pr/ with page objects, or a Django test on CommonRhinoTestCase.

Then the harness, not the model, runs them on the unchanged code. Each must fail on an assertion, not on an import or syntax error. A test that fails because a component does not exist yet proves nothing. That run is saved as the "before" evidence.

Now the lock. A digest is a short fingerprint of a file's bytes; sha256 is the algorithm. The harness stores one digest per test file in /work/.nova/locked.json, outside the checkout, so a git command cannot touch it.
sections.because: A test written after the code tends to test what the code does; showing it fail first proves it can fail.

notes.text: createHash from node:crypto. No library needed for sha256.
The checkout is always /work/fcp (lesson g3-9), so relative paths are stable.
The lock file lives outside the checkout. Nova's git and Bash work in /work/fcp.
digest reads the file's bytes and returns the sha256 as hex text.
locked reads the lock file, or returns an empty map before the lock exists.
lock is called once, after every QA test was shown red. It writes { path: digest } for each file.

sections.h: The hook that denies, and the Stop hook that re-checks
p: denyLockedEdits is a PreToolUse hook (lesson p8-4) on Edit and Write. It resolves the tool's file path, makes it relative to the repo, and looks it up in the lock. A locked file gets a calm deny with an alternative. Add a new test, or ask the requester to change the QA plan.

Bash can write files the hook never sees, for example sed -i. So the Stop hook calls changedLockedFiles, which re-hashes every locked file. A changed or missing file means Nova is not done. G0's CI check and the scope judge (lesson g4-4) are the outer layers of the same wall.
If the QA plan itself was wrong, Nova asks the requester to change it. A new approval unlocks and re-locks with the new tests.
sections.because: The hook gives an early, readable refusal; the re-hash at Stop makes sure no path around it exists.

notes.text: Registered under PreToolUse with matcher "Edit|Write", so it runs before either tool touches a file.
Both tools pass file_path. Other tools have none, and the hook lets them through.
Not locked: return {} and the edit proceeds. Object.hasOwn avoids a prototype lookup.
permissionDecision "deny" stops the tool call. The model sees the reason as the tool's answer.
The reason names the alternative. A refusal with a way forward keeps the run moving.
A file is changed if it is gone or its digest differs from the one stored at lock time.
The list of changed locked files. Empty means the wall held; anything else blocks done.

callout.text: Nova may add tests. It may never change the tests it is judged by. The hook, the Stop re-hash, G0's locked-checks CI check and the scope judge all enforce the same rule.

p: Put the four tickets in run order. Nova plans and writes the QA plan. The QA agent co-signs it. The requester approves done and the checks together (lesson g4-2).

Then Nova writes the tests, the harness runs them red and locks them. Only now does Nova write code, picking its checks from the guide and recording them in checks.json. At Stop, every QA check needs a passing run and proof, and every locked file must be unchanged.
The ticket order in Jira is different. The guide (G4-08) and check selection (G4-15) come first, because the lock (G4-16) and the co-sign (G4-13) build on them.

callout.text: When you read a Nova PR, start with the checks table. It is built from checks.json, so it shows what Nova ran, why, and what it chose to skip.

lab.title: Trace a QA check from plan to lock (reading lab)

worked.do: Open g4.json, find G4-16 and read how 2. Answer: who runs the new tests the first time, Nova or the harness?
worked.see: The harness. Each test must fail on an assertion, not an import error, and that run is the "before" evidence.

worked.do: Trace QA-2 through three places: plan.json qa_plan, checks.json ran[].qa_check, and the PR table.
worked.see: QA-2 is the user_sees line in the plan, the command that proved it in checks.json, and one row in How it was checked.

worked.do: In locked-checks.ts part 2, predict denyLockedEdits for file_path /work/fcp/frontend/src/App.tsx when only frontend/test/unit/projects.test.tsx is locked.
worked.see: {} (an empty object). The path is not in locked.json, so the edit is allowed.

worked.do: Predict what happens when Nova runs sed -i on a locked test through Bash.
worked.see: The PreToolUse hook sees no file_path, so the edit happens. At Stop, changedLockedFiles() lists the file and Nova is not done until it is restored.

worked.do: Read G4-13 how 2. What happens when Nova and the QA agent still disagree after one revision?
worked.see: Both views go into the plan message and the requester decides (lesson g4-2).

lab.faded: Write checks.json by hand for a CSS-only change. Use kind fe_bug, services_started [] and two runs (npm run lint, npm run check-types), with a why each. One skip is left for you: the browser run, with the reason you would give a reviewer.
lab.alone: Write the 3 eval cases G4-08 asks for, as one line each. They are a CSS-only change, a shared component used on many pages, and a serializer field rename. For each, say the starting checks and the sign to look deeper.
lab.done: For any QA check, you can say where it is written, who runs it red and what locks it. You can also say what catches an edit around the lock.

quiz.q: Who runs the QA tests on the unchanged code the first time, and why?

options.text: Nova, so it can fix any test that fails to import
options.why: A test that fails on an import proves nothing. Nova must fix such a test, but the harness is what runs the red step.

options.text: The harness, so the red run is evidence Nova did not produce
options.why: The harness runs them, requires an assertion failure, and saves the run as the "before" evidence.

options.text: The QA agent, as part of the co-sign
options.why: The co-sign happens before approval and reads only the ticket and the QA plan; it runs nothing.
Adding tests is always allowed. The deny reason even suggests it.

options.text: Nova changing the tests it is judged by
options.why: The hook denies Edit and Write on locked files, and the Stop hook re-hashes to catch Bash edits.

options.text: The requester changing the QA plan
options.why: The requester can change it; a new approval unlocks and re-locks with the new tests.

quiz.q: What does the QA agent see when it co-signs?

options.text: The whole plan and Nova's notes, so it has context
options.why: That is exactly what it must not see, or it could be talked into agreeing.

options.text: The ticket text, the QA plan and the screen states only
options.why: A tester who never saw Nova's reasoning catches checks that would pass on a broken build.

options.text: The diff, so it can judge the tests
options.why: There is no diff yet. The co-sign happens before any code is written.

words.plain: A reference page in the verify skill: where to start checking, when to look deeper, what proof fits.
Nova's recorded choice of checks to run and skip, with a reason each, in .nova/checks.json.
A short fingerprint of a file's bytes; sha256 is the algorithm we use.
A QA test whose digest is stored, so any change to it is denied or caught at Stop.
The QA agent's signature on the QA plan, saying the checks would fail on a broken build.
The saved run that shows each QA test failing on the unchanged code.
